```{r, eval=FALSE}
sce.pbmc <- runUMAP(sce.pbmc, dimred="PCA")

## Graph-based clustering---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(scran)
nn.clusters <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA") 
# returns a vector containing cluster assignments for each cell in our SingleCellExperiment object
# By default, clusterCells() uses the 10 nearest neighbors of each cell to construct a shared nearest neighbor graph
# Edge weight is defined by the highest average rank of the shared neighbors
# The Walktrap method from the igraph package is used to identify communities
table(nn.clusters)

library(scater)
colLabels(sce.pbmc) <- nn.clusters # adding cluster assignments as a factor to each cell
plotReducedDim(sce.pbmc, "TSNE", colour_by="label")

# Similar to the above, this is a more verbose call
library(bluster)
nn.clusters2 <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=SNNGraphParam(k=10, type="rank", cluster.fun="walktrap"))
table(nn.clusters2)

nn.clust.info <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", full=TRUE) # returns all intermediate structures that are used during clustering, including a graph object from the igraph package
nn.clust.info$objects$graph

set.seed(11000)
reducedDim(sce.pbmc, "force") <- igraph::layout_with_fr(nn.clust.info$objects$graph) # visualizing the graph using a force-directed layout
plotReducedDim(sce.pbmc, colour_by="label", dimred="force")

## Adjusting the parameters---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Adjusting the number of neighbors (k)
# More resolved.
clust.5 <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(k=5))
table(clust.5)
# Less resolved.
clust.50 <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(k=50))
table(clust.50)

# Adjusting the edge weighting scheme
# number: Weight edges based on the number of nearest neighbors that are shared between two cells
clust.num <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(type="number"))
table(clust.num)
# jaccard: Weight edges according to the Jaccard index of the two sets of neighbors
clust.jaccard <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(type="jaccard"))
table(clust.jaccard)
# disabling weighting altogether
clust.none <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=KNNGraphParam())
table(clust.none)

# Using different community detection algorithms
clust.walktrap <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(cluster.fun="walktrap"))

clust.louvain <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(cluster.fun="louvain"))

clust.infomap <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(cluster.fun="infomap"))

clust.fast <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(cluster.fun="fast_greedy"))

clust.labprop <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(cluster.fun="label_prop"))

clust.eigen <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=NNGraphParam(cluster.fun="leading_eigen"))

# Comparing clustering strategies and visualizing them in a heatmap
library(pheatmap)

# Using a large pseudo-count for a smoother color transition
# between 0 and 1 cell in each 'tab'.
tab <- table(paste("Infomap", clust.infomap), 
    paste("Walktrap", clust.walktrap))
ivw <- pheatmap(log10(tab+10), main="Infomap vs Walktrap",
    color=viridis::viridis(100), silent=TRUE)

tab <- table(paste("Fast", clust.fast), 
    paste("Walktrap", clust.walktrap))
fvw <- pheatmap(log10(tab+10), main="Fast-greedy vs Walktrap",
    color=viridis::viridis(100), silent=TRUE)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(ivw[[4]], fvw[[4]])
# Infomap yields finer clusters than Walktrap while fast-greedy yields coarser clusters
# scran by default uses rank-based weights followed by Walktrap clustering
# seurat by default uses Jaccard-based weights followed by Louvain clustering

## Vector quantization with k-means-----------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(100)
clust.kmeans <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=KmeansParam(centers=10))
table(clust.kmeans)
colLabels(sce.pbmc) <- clust.kmeans
plotReducedDim(sce.pbmc, "TSNE", colour_by="label") # t-SNE being a graph based algorithm will agree more with graph-based clustering than k-means

# A reasonable choice of k can be obtained by computing the gap statistic using methods from the cluster package. A more practical use is to deliberately set k to a large value to achieve overclustering. This will forcibly partition cells inside broad clusters that do not have well-defined internal structure.
set.seed(100)
clust.kmeans2 <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA", 
    BLUSPARAM=KmeansParam(centers=20))
table(clust.kmeans2)
colLabels(sce.pbmc) <- clust.kmeans2
plotTSNE(sce.pbmc, colour_by="label", text_by="label")

# For larger datasets, we can use a variant of this approach named mini-batch k-means from the mbkmeans package. At each iteration, we only update the cluster assignments and centroid positions for a small subset of the observations. This reduces memory usage and computational time and supports parallelization via BiocParallel.
library(mbkmeans)
set.seed(100)
clust.mbkmeans <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA",
    BLUSPARAM=bluster::MbkmeansParam(centers=10))
table(clust.mbkmeans)

# k-means when used for vector quantization overcomes many limitation of directly using k-means
set.seed(0101010)
kgraph.clusters <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA",
    BLUSPARAM=TwoStepParam(
        first=KmeansParam(centers=1000),
        second=NNGraphParam(k=5)
    )
)
table(kgraph.clusters)
plotTSNE(sce.pbmc, colour_by=I(kgraph.clusters)) # uses the external vector as it is

## Hierarchical clustering----------------------------------------------------------------------------
sce.416b <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.416b_processed.rds")

# Performs hierarchical clustering on the top PCs i.e., computes a cell-cell distance matrix using the top PCs
# then applies Ward’s minimum variance method to obtain a dendrogram
# Here, Ward's methods is more appropriate as it is less affected by differences in variance between clusters
library(scran)
library(bluster)
library(scater)

hclust.416b <- clusterCells(sce.416b, use.dimred="PCA",
    BLUSPARAM=HclustParam(method="ward.D2"), full=TRUE)
tree.416b <- hclust.416b$objects$hclust

# Making a prettier dendrogram.
library(dendextend)
tree.416b$labels <- seq_along(tree.416b$labels)
dend <- as.dendrogram(tree.416b, hang=0.1)

combined.fac <- paste0(sce.416b$block, ".", sub(" .*", "", sce.416b$phenotype))
labels_colors(dend) <- c(
    "20160113.wild"="blue",
    "20160113.induced"="red",
    "20160325.wild"="dodgerblue",
    "20160325.induced"="salmon"
)[combined.fac][order.dendrogram(dend)]

# Each leaf node is a cell that is coloured according to its oncogene induction status (red is induced, blue is control) and plate of origin (light or dark).
# There is a clear split in the population caused by oncogene induction.
plot(dend)

# dynamicTreeCut is used to remove internal branches such that every subtree represents a distinct cluster
# deepSplit is used to control the resolution of the resulting clusters
hclust.dyn <- clusterCells(sce.416b, use.dimred="PCA",
    BLUSPARAM=HclustParam(method="ward.D2", cut.dynamic=TRUE,
        cut.params=list(minClusterSize=10, deepSplit=1)))
table(hclust.dyn)
labels_colors(dend) <- as.integer(hclust.dyn)[order.dendrogram(dend)]
# Each leaf node is a cell that is coloured according to its assigned cluster identity from a dynamic tree cut.
plot(dend)

colLabels(sce.416b) <- factor(hclust.dyn)
# Cluster 2 is split across two visual clusters in the plot but this might be due to a distortion introduced by t-SNE, given that this cluster actually has the highest average silhouette width
plotReducedDim(sce.416b, "TSNE", colour_by="label")

## In two-step procedures------------------------------------------------------
# We can use a two-step approach to perform hierarchical clustering on the representative centroids.
# This avoids the construction of a distance matrix across all cells for faster computation.
# Setting the seed due to the randomness of k-means.
sce.pbmc <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.pbmc_processed.rds")

set.seed(1111)
khclust.info <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA",
    BLUSPARAM=TwoStepParam(
        first=KmeansParam(centers=1000),
        second=HclustParam(method="ward.D2", cut.dynamic=TRUE,
            cut.param=list(deepSplit=3)) # for higher resolution.
    ),
    full=TRUE
)
table(khclust.info$clusters)

# t-SNE plot of the PBMC dataset, where each point represents a cell and is coloured according to the identity of the assigned cluster from combined k-means/hierarchical clustering.
plotTSNE(sce.pbmc, colour_by = I(khclust.info$clusters), 
    text_by = I(khclust.info$clusters))

# To examine the dendrogram constructed on the centroids
k.stats <- khclust.info$objects$first # k-means statistics
tree.pbmc <- khclust.info$objects$second$hclust # hclust statistics

m <- match(as.integer(tree.pbmc$labels), k.stats$kmeans$cluster)
final.clusters <- khclust.info$clusters[m]

# TODO: expose scater color palette for easier re-use,
# given that the default colors start getting recycled.
dend <- as.dendrogram(tree.pbmc, hang=0.1)
labels_colors(dend) <- as.integer(final.clusters)[order.dendrogram(dend)]

# Dendrogram of the k-mean centroids after hierarchical clustering in the PBMC dataset. Each leaf node represents a representative cluster of cells generated by k-mean clustering.
plot(dend)

# Another method of using the k-means centroids to clustering by affinity propagation
# Each data point repeatedly decides which data point best represents it based on similarity and group agreement, and clusters emerge as groups of points choosing the same representative.
# Setting the seed due to the randomness of k-means.
set.seed(1111)
kaclust.info <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA",
    BLUSPARAM=TwoStepParam(
        first=KmeansParam(centers=1000),
        second=AffinityParam(q=0.1) # larger q => more clusters
    ),
    full=TRUE
)
table(kaclust.info$clusters)

# Each point represents a cell and is coloured according to the identity of the assigned cluster from combined k-means/affinity propagation clustering.
plotTSNE(sce.pbmc, colour_by=I(kaclust.info$clusters), 
    text_by=I(kaclust.info$clusters))

## Subclustering-----------------------------------------------------------------
# Improves resolution by repeating the feature selection and clustering within a single cluster.
# It aims to select HVGs and PCs that are more relevant to internal structure, improving resolution by avoiding noise from unnecessary features.
clust.full <- clusterCells(sce.pbmc, use.dimred="PCA")

# Distribution of log-normalized expression values for several T cell markers within each cluster in the 10X PBMC dataset. Each cluster is color-coded for convenience.
plotExpression(sce.pbmc, features=c("CD3E", "CCR7", "CD69", "CD44"),
    x=I(clust.full), colour_by=I(clust.full))

# Repeating modelling and PCA on the subset.
memory <- 6L # L for explicitly storing 6 as an integer rather than floating point numeric
sce.memory <- sce.pbmc[,clust.full==memory]
dec.memory <- modelGeneVar(sce.memory)
sce.memory <- denoisePCA(sce.memory, technical=dec.memory,
    subset.row=getTopHVGs(dec.memory, n=5000))

# Applying graph-based clustering within this memory subset to obtain CD4+ and CD8+ subclusters
g.memory <- buildSNNGraph(sce.memory, use.dimred="PCA")
clust.memory <- igraph::cluster_walktrap(g.memory)$membership

# Distribution of CD4 and CD8A log-normalized expression values within each cluster in the memory T cell subset of the 10X PBMC dataset.
plotExpression(sce.memory, features=c("CD8A", "CD4"),
    x=I(factor(clust.memory)))

# Performing automatic sub-clustering of cells inside already identified clusters of a SingleCellExperiment object
set.seed(1000010)
subcluster.out <- quickSubCluster(sce.pbmc, groups=clust.full,
    prepFUN=function(x) { # Preparing the subsetted SCE for clustering.
        dec <- modelGeneVar(x)
        input <- denoisePCA(x, technical=dec,
            subset.row=getTopHVGs(dec, prop=0.1),
            BSPARAM=BiocSingular::IrlbaParam())
    },
    clusterFUN=function(x) { # Performing the subclustering in the subset.
        g <- buildSNNGraph(x, use.dimred="PCA", k=20)
        igraph::cluster_walktrap(g)$membership
    }
)

# One SingleCellExperiment object per parent cluster:
names(subcluster.out)

# Looking at the subclustering for one example:
table(subcluster.out[[1]]$subcluster)
```

## Marker gene detection
- We have a priori knowledge of the marker genes associated with particular cell types, allowing us to treat clustering as a proxy for cell type identity.
- The most straightforward approach to marker gene detection involves testing for differential expression between clusters. If a gene is strongly DE between clusters, it is likely to have driven the separation of cells in the clustering algorithm.
- **Scoring markers by pairwise comparisons:**
    - It compares each pair of clusters and compute scores quantifying the differences in the expression distributions between clusters.
    - Marker detection works better when clusters are compared pairwise rather than against all other cells, because this avoids biases from uneven cell-type abundances. 
    - Effect sizes (like log-fold change) are more informative than p-values in single-cell data, so modern methods like scoreMarkers() focus on effect sizes instead of statistical significance.
    - The AUC or Cohen’s d is usually the best choice for general purpose marker detection, as they are effective regardless of the magnitude of the expression values. The log-fold change in the detected proportion is specifically useful for identifying binary changes in expression.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sce.pbmc <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.pbmc_processed.rds")

## Scoring markers by pairwise comparisons--------------------------------------------------
library(scran)
marker.info <- scoreMarkers(sce.pbmc, colLabels(sce.pbmc))
marker.info
# The different effect size summaries include:
# self.average: mean log-expression of the gene in a particular cluster
# other.averag: grand mean across all other clusters
# self.detected: the proportion of cells with detected expression in the cluster
# other.detected: the mean detected proportion of cells across all other clusters
colnames(marker.info[["5"]]) # statistics for cluster 5.

# For each cluster, we can then rank candidate markers based on one of these effect size summaries.
# Cluster 5 contains NK cells
chosen <- marker.info[["5"]]
ordered <- chosen[order(chosen$mean.AUC, decreasing=TRUE),]
head(ordered[,1:4]) # showing basic stats only, for brevity.

library(scater)
# Distribution of expression values across clusters for the top potential marker genes (as determined by the mean AUC) for cluster 5 in the PBMC dataset.
plotExpression(sce.pbmc, features=head(rownames(ordered)), 
    x="label", colour_by="label")

## Effect sizes for pairwise comparisons--------------------------------------------------
# In the context of marker detection, the area under the curve (AUC) quantifies our ability to distinguish between two distributions in a pairwise comparison. 
# The AUC represents the probability that a randomly chosen observation from our cluster of interest is greater than a randomly chosen observation from the other cluster. 
# A value of 1 corresponds to upregulation, where all values of our cluster of interest are greater than any value from the other cluster.
# A value of 0.5 means that there is no net difference in the location of the distributions.
# A value of 0 corresponds to downregulation. 
# The AUC is closely related to the U statistic in the Wilcoxon ranked sum test (a.k.a., Mann-Whitney U-test).
auc.only <- chosen[,grepl("AUC", colnames(chosen))]
auc.only[order(auc.only$mean.AUC,decreasing=TRUE),]

# Cohen’s d is a standardized log-fold change where the difference in the mean log-expression between groups is scaled by the average standard deviation across groups.
# Positive values indicate that the gene is upregulated in our cluster of interest, negative values indicate downregulation and values close to zero indicate that there is little difference. # Cohen’s d is roughly analogous to the t-statistic in various two-sample t-tests.
cohen.only <- chosen[,grepl("logFC.cohen", colnames(chosen))]
cohen.only[order(cohen.only$mean.logFC.cohen,decreasing=TRUE),]

# Log-fold change in the proportion of cells with detected expression between clusters is also calculated.
# This ignores any information about the magnitude of expression, only considering whether any expression is detected at all.
# Positive values indicate that a greater proportion of cells express the gene in our cluster of interest compared to the other cluster.
# A pseudo-count is added to avoid undefined log-fold changes when no cells express the gene in either group.
detect.only <- chosen[,grepl("logFC.detected", colnames(chosen))]
detect.only[order(detect.only$mean.logFC.detected,decreasing=TRUE),]

## Summarizing pairwise effects-----------------------------------------------------------
# For N clusters, each cluster is associated with N - 1 values for each type of effect size.
# Mean: 
# For cluster X, a large mean effect size (>0 for LFC, >0.5 for AUCs) indicates that the gene is upregulated in X compared to the average of the other groups.
# Median: 
# A large value indicates that the gene is upregulated in X compared to most (>50 %) other clusters.
# The median provides greater robustness to outliers than the mean. It avoids an inflated effect size if only a minority of comparisons have large effects, but it also overstates the effect size by ignoring a minority of comparisons that have opposing effects.
# The minimum value (min.*) is the most stringent summary for identifying upregulated genes, as a large value indicates that the gene is upregulated in X compared to all other clusters. Conversely, if the minimum is small (<0 for the log-fold changes, <0.5 for the AUCs), we can conclude that the gene is downregulated in X compared to at least one other cluster.
# The maximum value (max.*) is the least stringent summary for identifying upregulated genes, as a large value can be obtained if there is strong upregulation in X compared to any other cluster. Conversely, if the maximum is small, we can conclude that the gene is downregulated in X compared to all other clusters.
# The minimum rank, a.k.a., “min-rank” (rank.*) is the smallest rank of each gene across all pairwise comparisons. Specifically, genes are ranked within each pairwise comparison based on decreasing effect size, and then the smallest rank across all comparisons is reported for each gene. If a gene has a small min-rank, we can conclude that it is one of the top upregulated genes in at least one comparison of X to another cluster.

# Using the median Cohen’s d to obtain a ranking of upregulated markers for cluster 12, which probably contains monocytes.
chosen <- marker.info[["12"]]
ordered <- chosen[order(chosen$median.logFC.cohen,decreasing=TRUE),]
head(ordered[,1:4])

# Distribution of expression values across clusters for the top potential marker genes (as determined by the median Cohen’s d) for cluster 12 in the PBMC dataset.
plotExpression(sce.pbmc, features=head(rownames(ordered)), 
    x="label", colour_by="label")

# Ranking by the minimum can be highly effective as it yields a concise set of highly cluster-specific markers. 
# However, any gene that is expressed at the same level in two or more clusters will simply not be detected. This is likely to discard many interesting genes, especially if the clusters are finely resolved with weak separation. 
# For example, consider a mixed population of CD4+ only, CD8+ only, double-positive and double-negative T cells. Neither C4 or Cd8 would be detected as subpopulation-specific markers because each gene is expressed in two subpopulations such that the minimum effect would be small.

# Ranking genes by the min-rank is similiar in stringency to ranking by the maximum effect size, in that both will respond to strong DE in a single comparison. 
# However, the min-rank is more useful as it ensures that a single comparison to another cluster with consistently large effects does not dominate the ranking. 
# If we select all genes with min-ranks less than or equal to T, the resulting set is the union of the top T genes from all pairwise comparisons. This guarantees that our set contains at least T genes that can distinguish our cluster of interest from any other cluster, which permits a comprehensive determination of a cluster’s identity.

ordered <- chosen[order(chosen$rank.logFC.cohen),]
top.ranked <- ordered[ordered$rank.logFC.cohen <= 5,]
rownames(top.ranked)

# Heatmap of the centered average log-expression values for the top potential marker genes for cluster 12 in the PBMC dataset. The set of markers was selected as those genes with Cohen’s d-derived min-ranks less than or equal to 5.
plotGroupedHeatmap(sce.pbmc, features=rownames(top.ranked), group="label", 
    center=TRUE, zlim=c(-3, 3))

# Our discussion above has focused mainly on potential markers that are upregulated in our cluster of interest. 
# However, it also means that any cluster defined by downregulation of a marker will not contain that gene among the top features. This is occasionally relevant for subtypes or other states that are defined by low expression of particular genes. 
# In such cases, focusing on upregulation may yield a disappointing set of markers, and it may be worth examining some of the lowest-ranked genes to see if there is any consistent downregulation compared to other clusters.

# Omitting the decreasing=TRUE to focus on negative effects.
ordered <- chosen[order(chosen$median.logFC.cohen),1:4]
head(ordered)

## Obtaining the full effects-------------------------------------------------------------
# To obtain the effect sizes for all pairwise comparisons involving a particular cluster, we set full.stats=TRUE
marker.info <- scoreMarkers(sce.pbmc, colLabels(sce.pbmc), full.stats=TRUE)
chosen <- marker.info[["12"]]
# full.AUC contains the AUCs for the comparisons between cluster 12 and every other cluster.
chosen$full.AUC

# To identify the genes that distinguish cluster 12 from other clusters with high LYZ expression
lyz.high <- c("7", "8", "10", "12", "15", "18") # based on inspection of the previous Figure.
subset <- chosen$full.AUC[,colnames(chosen$full.AUC) %in% lyz.high]
to.show <- subset[computeMinRank(subset) <= 10,]
to.show

# Heatmap of the centered average log-expression values for the top potential marker genes for cluster 12 relative to other LYZ-high clusters in the PBMC dataset. The set of markers was selected as those genes with AUC-derived min-ranks less than or equal to 10.
plotGroupedHeatmap(sce.pbmc[,colLabels(sce.pbmc) %in% lyz.high],
    features=rownames(to.show), group="label", center=TRUE, zlim=c(-3, 3))

# To identify markers that are upregulated against 80 % of other clusters
# Computing and sorting on the 20th percentile of effect sizes
stat <- rowQuantiles(as.matrix(chosen$full.AUC), p=0.2)
chosen[order(stat, decreasing=TRUE), 1:4]

## Using a log-fold change threshold---------------------------------------------------------
# The Cohen’s d and AUC calculations consider both the magnitude of the difference between clusters as well as the variability within each cluster.
# If the variability is lower, it is possible for a gene to have a large effect size even if the magnitude of the difference is small. These genes tend to be somewhat uninformative for cell type identification despite their strong differential expression (e.g., ribosomal protein genes).
# Cohen's d = difference in means (magnitude) / within-group variability (SD)
# Small difference, Low variability; d = 0.1/0.05 = 2 (Large effect size)
# Large difference, High variability; d = 2/3 = 0.67 (Small effect size)
# We would prefer genes with larger log-fold changes between clusters, even if they have higher variability.

# To favor the detection of such genes, we can compute the effect sizes relative to a log-fold change threshold by setting lfc= in scoreMarkers().
# The definition of Cohen’s d is generalized to the standardized difference between the observed log-fold change and the specified lfc threshold.
# The AUC is redefined as the probability of randomly picking an expression value from one cluster that is greater than a random value from the other cluster plus lfc.
marker.info.lfc <- scoreMarkers(sce.pbmc, colLabels(sce.pbmc), lfc=2)
chosen2 <- marker.info.lfc[["4"]]
chosen2 <- chosen2[order(chosen2$mean.AUC, decreasing=TRUE),]
chosen2[,c("self.average", "other.average", "mean.AUC")]

# Dot plot of the top potential marker genes (as determined by the mean AUC) for cluster 4 in the PBMC dataset. Each row corrresponds to a marker gene and each column corresponds to a cluster. The size of each dot represents the proportion of cells with detected expression of the gene in the cluster, while the color is proportional to the average expression across all cells in that cluster.
plotDots(sce.pbmc, rownames(chosen2)[1:10], group="label")

# If lfc is positive, a positive Cohen’s d and an AUC above 0.5 represents upregulation. 
# However, a negative Cohen’s d or AUC below 0.5 may not represent downregulation; it may just indicate that the observed log-fold change is less than the specified lfc. 
# The converse applies when lfc is negative, where the only conclusive interpretation occurs for downregulated genes.

## Handling blocking factors---------------------------------------------------------------
# Factors of variation like batch effects, sex differences if not modelled, can interfere with marker gene detection.
# By inflating the variance within each cluster, but also by distorting the log-fold changes if the cluster composition varies across levels of the blocking factor.
sce.416b <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.416b_processed.rds")
m.out <- scoreMarkers(sce.416b, colLabels(sce.416b), block=sce.416b$block)

# For each gene, each pairwise comparison between clusters is performed separately in each level of the blocking factor - in this case, the plate of origin. 
# By comparing within each batch, we cancel out any batch effects so that they are not conflated with the biological differences between subpopulations. 
# The effect sizes are then averaged across batches to obtain a single value per comparison, using a weighted mean that accounts for the number of cells involved in the comparison in each batch. 
# A similar correction is applied to the mean log-expression and proportion of detected cells inside and outside each cluster.
demo <- m.out[["1"]]
ordered <- demo[order(demo$median.logFC.cohen, decreasing=TRUE),]
ordered[,1:4]

# Distribution of expression values across clusters for the top potential marker genes from cluster 1 in the 416B dataset. Each point represents a cell and is colored by the batch of origin.
plotExpression(sce.416b, features=rownames(ordered)[1:6],
    x="label", colour_by="block")

# The block= argument assumes that each pair of clusters is present in at least one batch. In scenarios where cells from two clusters never co-occur in the same batch, the associated pairwise comparison will be impossible and is ignored during calculation of summary statistics.
```

## Cell type annotation
- **Strategies of cell-annotation:**
    - Using curated gene sets associated with particular biological processes e.g. from GO and KEGG.
    - Comparing the expression profiles to published reference datasets where each sample or cell has already been annotated with its putative biological state by domain experts.
- **Assigning cell labels from reference data:**
    - Labels can be assigned to each cell in our uncharacterized dataset based on the most similar reference sample (using ml methods like random forests and support vector machines).
    - **SingleR** method assigns labels to cells based on the reference samples with the highest Spearman rank correlations, using only the marker genes between pairs of labels to focus on the relevant differences between cell types. It also performs a fine-tuning step for each cell where the correlations are recomputed with just the marker genes for the top-scoring labels.
    - Analysis is restricted by the diversity and resolution of the available labels which is overcome by de novo identification of clusters.
- **Assigning cell labels from gene sets:**
  - Uses explicitly identifiable sets of marker genes that are highly expressed in each individual cell

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Assigning cell labels from reference data---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Using existing references

# It is possible to run SingleR on the raw counts without any a priori quality control
sce.pbmc <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.pbmc_processed.rds")

# Celldex contains a number of curated reference datasets, assembled from bulk RNA-seq or microarray data of sorted cell types
# These are good enough provided they contain the cell types that are expected in the test population
library(celldex)
ref <- BlueprintEncodeData()

library(SingleR)
pred <- SingleR(test=sce.pbmc, ref=ref, labels=ref$label.main)
# Returns a dataframe where each row correspond to a cell in the test dataset and contains its label assignments
# We can also use the labels in ref$label.fine which provides more resolution at the cost of speed and increased ambiguity in the assignments
table(pred$labels)

# Ideally, each cell should exhibit a high score in one label relative to all of the others, indicating that the assignment to that label was unambiguous.
# Heatmap of the assignment score for each cell (column) and label (row). Scores are shown before any fine-tuning and are normalized to [0, 1] within each cell.
plotScoreHeatmap(pred)
# Several clusters are nested within the monocyte and B cell labels, indicating that the clustering represents finer subdivisions within the cell types.
# The clustering does not effectively distinguish between CD4+ and CD8+ T cell labels due to the presence of other factors of heterogeneity within the T cell subpopulation (e.g., activation) that have a stronger influence on unsupervised methods than the CD4+/CD8+ distinction.

library(SingleCellExperiment)
tab <- table(Assigned=pred$pruned.labels, Cluster=colLabels(sce.pbmc))

# Adding a pseudo-count of 10 to avoid strong color jumps with just 1 cell.
library(pheatmap)
# Heatmap of the distribution of cells across labels and clusters in the 10X PBMC dataset. Color scale is reported in the log10-number of cells for each cluster-label combination.
pheatmap(log2(tab+10), color=colorRampPalette(c("white", "blue"))(101))

## Using custom references
# Using datasets that were manually annotated previously to annotate a new dataset in an automated manner
# Using sce.muraro dataset as our reference
sce.muraro <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.muraro_processed.rds")

# Pruning out unknown or unclear labels.
sce.muraro <- sce.muraro[,!is.na(sce.muraro$label) & 
    sce.muraro$label!="unclear"]
table(sce.muraro$label)

# Assigning labels to our test dataset (Segerstolpe)
sce.seger <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.seger_processed.rds")

library(ensembldb)
hs.db <- EnsDb("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Workflows/EnsDb_Hsapiens_v97.sqlite")
# Converting to FPKM for a more like-for-like comparison to UMI counts.
# However, results are often still good even when this step is skipped.
hs.exons <- exonsBy(hs.db, by="gene")
hs.exons <- GenomicRanges::reduce(hs.exons)
hs.len <- sum(width(hs.exons))

library(scuttle)
available <- intersect(rownames(sce.seger), names(hs.len))
fpkm.seger <- calculateFPKM(sce.seger[available,], hs.len[available])

pred.seger <- SingleR(test=fpkm.seger, ref=sce.muraro, 
    labels=sce.muraro$label, de.method="wilcox")
table(pred.seger$labels)

# As our test dataset also contains independently defined labels, we see a strong consistency between the two sets of labels, indicating that our automatic annotation is comparable to that generated manually by domain experts
tab <- table(pred.seger$pruned.labels, sce.seger$CellType)

# Heatmap of the confusion matrix between the predicted labels (rows) and the independently defined labels (columns) in the Segerstolpe dataset. The color is proportinal to the log-transformed number of cells with a given combination of labels from each set.
library(pheatmap)
pheatmap(log2(tab+10), color=colorRampPalette(c("white", "blue"))(101))

# Given a single-cell reference dataset, is it better to use it directly or convert it to pseudo-bulk values?
# A single-cell reference preserves the “shape” of the subpopulation in high-dimensional expression space, potentially yielding more accurate predictions when the differences between labels are subtle.
# However, it also requires more computational work to assign each cell in the test dataset.

## Assigning cell labels from gene sets------------------------------------------------------------------------------

```

# OSCA Workflows

## Lun 416B cell line (Smart-seq2)
- 416b: immortalized mouse myeloid progenitor cell line
- Contains two 96-well plates of 416b cells processed using the Smart-seq2 protocol
- A constant amount of spike-in RNA from the External RNA Controls Consortium (ERCC) was also added to each cell's lysate prior to library preparation.
- Expression of each gene was quantified by counting the total number of reads mapped to the exonic regions of the genome.
- Quantity of each spike-in transcript was measured by counting the number of reads mapped to the spike-in reference sequences.

```{r}
## Data loading---------------------------------------------------------------
library(scRNAseq)
sce.416b <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.416b.rds")
# Turning each block (2) as factors
sce.416b$block <- factor(sce.416b$block)

# Renaming the rows of our SingleCellExperiment with gene symbols
# Keeping ensembl identifiers for missing or duplicate gene symbols
library(AnnotationHub)
# ens.mm.v97 <- AnnotationHub()[["AH73905"]]
# file.copy(
#   DBI::dbGetInfo(dbconn(ens.mm.v97))$dbname,
#   "OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Workflows/ens.mm.v97.sqlite"
# )
ens.mm.v97 <- EnsDb("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Workflows/ens.mm.v97.sqlite")
rowData(sce.416b)$ENSEMBL <- rownames(sce.416b)
# Gene symbols
rowData(sce.416b)$SYMBOL <- mapIds(ens.mm.v97, keys=rownames(sce.416b),
    keytype="GENEID", column="SYMBOL")
# Chromosome
rowData(sce.416b)$SEQNAME <- mapIds(ens.mm.v97, keys=rownames(sce.416b),
    keytype="GENEID", column="SEQNAME")

library(scater)
rownames(sce.416b) <- uniquifyFeatureNames(rowData(sce.416b)$ENSEMBL, 
    rowData(sce.416b)$SYMBOL)

## Quality Control-----------------------------------------------------------
# Saving an unfiltered copy of the SingleCellExperiment
unfiltered <- sce.416b

# calculating mitochondrial proportions (although not required as spike-ins are present for the same purpose)
mito <- which(rowData(sce.416b)$SEQNAME=="MT")
stats <- perCellQCMetrics(sce.416b, subsets=list(Mt=mito))
qc <- quickPerCellQC(stats, percent_subsets=c("subsets_Mt_percent",
    "altexps_ERCC_percent"), batch=sce.416b$block)
sce.416b <- sce.416b[,!qc$discard]

colData(unfiltered) <- cbind(colData(unfiltered), stats)
unfiltered$block <- factor(unfiltered$block)
unfiltered$discard <- qc$discard

# Distribution of each QC metric across cells in the 416B dataset, stratified by the plate of origin. Each point represents a cell and is colored according to whether that cell was discarded.
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="block", y="sum", 
        colour_by="discard") + scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Total count"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="block", y="detected", 
        colour_by="discard") + scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Detected features"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="block", y="subsets_Mt_percent", 
        colour_by="discard") + ggtitle("Mito percent"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="block", y="altexps_ERCC_percent", 
        colour_by="discard") + ggtitle("ERCC percent"),
    nrow=2,
    ncol=2
)

# Percentage of mitochondrial reads in each cell in the 416B dataset, compared to the total count (left) or the percentage of spike-in reads (right). Each point represents a cell and is colored according to whether that cell was discarded.
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="sum", y="subsets_Mt_percent", 
        colour_by="discard") + scale_x_log10(),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="altexps_ERCC_percent", y="subsets_Mt_percent",
        colour_by="discard"),
    ncol=2
)

# Number of cells removed and their reasons
colSums(as.matrix(qc))

## Normalization---------------------------------------------------------
# No pre-clustering is performed here, as the dataset is small and all cells are derived from the same cell line anyway.
library(scran)
sce.416b <- computeSumFactors(sce.416b)
sce.416b <- logNormCounts(sce.416b)
summary(sizeFactors(sce.416b))

# Relationship between the library size factors and the deconvolution size factors in the 416B dataset. Each cell is colored according to its oncogene induction status.
# The induced cells have size factors that are systematically shifted from the uninduced cells, consistent with the presence of a composition bias
plot(librarySizeFactors(sce.416b), sizeFactors(sce.416b), pch=16,
    xlab="Library size factors", ylab="Deconvolution factors", 
    col=c("black", "red")[grepl("induced", sce.416b$phenotype)+1],
    log="xy")

## Variance Modelling-----------------------------------------------------
# Blocks used to minimize plate effects
dec.416b <- modelGeneVarWithSpikes(sce.416b, "ERCC", block=sce.416b$block)
# Using the top 10% genes with the largest biological components
chosen.hvgs <- getTopHVGs(dec.416b, prop=0.1)

# Per-gene variance as a function of the mean for the log-expression values in the 416B dataset. Each point represents a gene (black) with the mean-variance trend (blue) fitted to the spike-in transcripts (red). This was performed separately for each plate.
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
blocked.stats <- dec.416b$per.block
for (i in colnames(blocked.stats)) {
    current <- blocked.stats[[i]]
    plot(current$mean, current$total, main=i, pch=16, cex=0.5,
        xlab="Mean of log-expression", ylab="Variance of log-expression")
    curfit <- metadata(current)
    points(curfit$mean, curfit$var, col="red", pch=16)
    curve(curfit$trend(x), col='dodgerblue', add=TRUE, lwd=2)
}

## Batch correction-----------------------------------------------------
# The composition of cells is expected to be the same across the two plates, hence the use of removeBatchEffect() rather than more complex methods. For larger datasets, use regressBatches() from the batchelor package.
library(limma)
assay(sce.416b, "corrected") <- removeBatchEffect(logcounts(sce.416b), 
    design=model.matrix(~sce.416b$phenotype), batch=sce.416b$block)

## Dimensionality reduction---------------------------------------------
# We do not expect a great deal of heterogeneity in this dataset, so we only request 10 PCs.
sce.416b <- runPCA(sce.416b, ncomponents=10, subset_row=chosen.hvgs,
    exprs_values="corrected", BSPARAM=BiocSingular::ExactParam())

# We use an exact SVD to avoid warnings from irlba about handling small datasets.
set.seed(1010)
sce.416b <- runTSNE(sce.416b, dimred="PCA", perplexity=10)

## Clustering-----------------------------------------------------------
my.dist <- dist(reducedDim(sce.416b, "PCA"))
my.tree <- hclust(my.dist, method="ward.D2")

library(dynamicTreeCut)
my.clusters <- unname(cutreeDynamic(my.tree, distM=as.matrix(my.dist),
    minClusterSize=10, verbose=0))
colLabels(sce.416b) <- factor(my.clusters)

# Each cluster is comprised of cells from both batches, indicating that the clustering is not driven by a batch effect.
table(Cluster=colLabels(sce.416b), Plate=sce.416b$block)

# We observe differences in in the composition of each cluster, consistent with a biological effect of oncogene induction.
table(Cluster=colLabels(sce.416b), Oncogene=sce.416b$phenotype)

# Each point represents a cell and is colored according to the assigned cluster.
plotTSNE(sce.416b, colour_by="label")

library(cluster)
clust.col <- scater:::.get_palette("tableau10medium") # hidden scater colours

# The silhouette score is a metric used to calculate the goodness of a clustering technique, ranging from -1 to +1, where a higher value indicates that objects are well-matched to their own cluster and poorly matched to neighboring clusters. It measures how similar a point is to its own cluster (cohesion) compared to other clusters (separation).
sil <- silhouette(my.clusters, dist = my.dist)

sil.cols <- clust.col[ifelse(sil[,3] > 0, sil[,1], sil[,2])]
sil.cols <- sil.cols[order(-sil[,1], sil[,3])]

# Most cells have relatively small positive widths indicating that the separation between clusters is weak. This may be symptomatic of over-clustering where clusters that are clearly defined on oncogene induction status are further split into subsets that are less well separated.
# Each bar represents the silhouette width for a cell and is colored according to the assigned cluster (if positive) or the closest cluster (if negative).
plot(sil, main = paste(length(unique(my.clusters)), "clusters"),
    border=sil.cols, col=sil.cols, do.col.sort=FALSE)

## Interpretation------------------------------------------------------------
markers <- findMarkers(sce.416b, my.clusters, block=sce.416b$block)
marker.set <- markers[["1"]]
head(marker.set, 10)

top.markers <- rownames(marker.set)[marker.set$Top <= 10]

# Expression profiles of the top candidates to verify that the DE signature is robust
# Most of the top markers have strong and consistent up- or downregulation in cells of cluster 1 compared to some or all of the other clusters.
# Cluster 1 contains oncogene-induced cells with strong downregulation of DNA replication and cell cycle genes. This is consistent with the potential induction of senescence as an anti-tumorigenic response.
plotHeatmap(sce.416b, features=top.markers, order_columns_by="label",
    colour_columns_by=c("label", "block", "phenotype"),
    center=TRUE, symmetric=TRUE, zlim=c(-5, 5))

## Saving the processed dataset-----------------------------------------------
saveRDS(sce.416b, "OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.416b_processed.rds")
```

```{r}
sce.zeisel <- aggregateAcrossFeatures(sce.zeisel,
```

## Unfiltered human PBMC (10X Genomics)

```{r}
## Data loading---------------------------------------------------------------
# library(DropletTestFiles)
# raw.path <- getTestFile("tenx-2.1.0-pbmc4k/1.0.0/raw.tar.gz")
# out.path <- file.path(tempdir(), "pbmc4k")
# untar(raw.path, exdir=out.path)

# library(DropletUtils)
# fname <- file.path(out.path, "raw_gene_bc_matrices/GRCh38")
# sce.pbmc <- read10xCounts(fname, col.names=TRUE)

sce.pbmc <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.pbmc.rds")

library(scater)
rownames(sce.pbmc) <- uniquifyFeatureNames(
    rowData(sce.pbmc)$ID, rowData(sce.pbmc)$Symbol)

library(EnsDb.Hsapiens.v86)
location <- mapIds(EnsDb.Hsapiens.v86, keys=rowData(sce.pbmc)$ID, 
    column="SEQNAME", keytype="GENEID")

## Quality control-----------------------------------------------------------
# Cell detection using the emptyDrops() algorithm
set.seed(100)
e.out <- emptyDrops(counts(sce.pbmc))
sce.pbmc <- sce.pbmc[,which(e.out$FDR <= 0.001)]

unfiltered <- sce.pbmc

# Removing cells with large mitochondrial proportions, using it as a proxy for cell damage. 
# This reduces the risk of removing cell types with low RNA content, especially in a heterogeneous PBMC population with many different cell types.
stats <- perCellQCMetrics(sce.pbmc, subsets=list(Mito=which(location=="MT")))
high.mito <- isOutlier(stats$subsets_Mito_percent, type="higher")
sce.pbmc <- sce.pbmc[,!high.mito]
summary(high.mito)

colData(unfiltered) <- cbind(colData(unfiltered), stats)
unfiltered$discard <- high.mito

# Each point is a cell and is colored according to whether it was discarded by the mitochondrial filter.
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotColData(unfiltered, y="sum", colour_by="discard") +
        scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Total count"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, y="detected", colour_by="discard") +
        scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Detected features"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, y="subsets_Mito_percent",
        colour_by="discard") + ggtitle("Mito percent"),
    ncol=2
)

# Proportion of mitochondrial reads in each cell of the PBMC dataset compared to its total count.
plotColData(unfiltered, x="sum", y="subsets_Mito_percent",
    colour_by="discard") + scale_x_log10()

## Normalization-------------------------------------------------------------
library(scran)
set.seed(1000)
clusters <- quickCluster(sce.pbmc)
sce.pbmc <- computeSumFactors(sce.pbmc, cluster=clusters)
sce.pbmc <- logNormCounts(sce.pbmc)

summary(sizeFactors(sce.pbmc))

plot(librarySizeFactors(sce.pbmc), sizeFactors(sce.pbmc), pch=16,
    xlab="Library size factors", ylab="Deconvolution factors", log="xy")

## Variance modelling---------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(1001)
dec.pbmc <- modelGeneVarByPoisson(sce.pbmc)
top.pbmc <- getTopHVGs(dec.pbmc, prop=0.1)

plot(dec.pbmc$mean, dec.pbmc$total, pch=16, cex=0.5,
    xlab="Mean of log-expression", ylab="Variance of log-expression")
curfit <- metadata(dec.pbmc)
curve(curfit$trend(x), col='dodgerblue', add=TRUE, lwd=2)

## Dimensionality reduction---------------------------------------------------
set.seed(10000)
sce.pbmc <- denoisePCA(sce.pbmc, subset.row=top.pbmc, technical=dec.pbmc)

set.seed(100000)
sce.pbmc <- runTSNE(sce.pbmc, dimred="PCA")

set.seed(1000000)
sce.pbmc <- runUMAP(sce.pbmc, dimred="PCA")

# Number of reasonable PCs retained
ncol(reducedDim(sce.pbmc, "PCA"))

## Clustering-----------------------------------------------------------------
g <- buildSNNGraph(sce.pbmc, k=10, use.dimred = 'PCA')
clust <- igraph::cluster_walktrap(g)$membership
colLabels(sce.pbmc) <- factor(clust)

table(colLabels(sce.pbmc))
plotTSNE(sce.pbmc, colour_by="label")

## Interpretation-------------------------------------------------------------
markers <- findMarkers(sce.pbmc, pval.type="some", direction="up")

# High expression of CD14, CD68 and MNDA combined with low expression of FCGR3A (CD16) suggests that this cluster contains monocytes, compared to macrophages in cluster 16
marker.set <- markers[["7"]]
as.data.frame(marker.set[1:30,1:3])

# Distribution of expression values for monocyte and macrophage markers across clusters in the PBMC dataset.
plotExpression(sce.pbmc, features=c("CD14", "CD68",
    "MNDA", "FCGR3A"), x="label", colour_by="label")

# Saving the processed dataset-----------------------------------------------
saveRDS(sce.pbmc, "OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.pbmc_processed.rds")
```

## Muraro human pancreas (CEL-seq)

```{r}
## Data loading------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(scRNAseq)
# sce.muraro <- MuraroPancreasData()
sce.muraro <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.muraro.rds")

# Converting back to Ensembl identifiers
# library(AnnotationHub)
# edb <- AnnotationHub()[["AH73881"]]

# Save the sqlite database
# db_path <- DBI::dbGetInfo(dbconn(edb))$dbname
# file.copy(db_path, "EnsDb_Hsapiens_v97.sqlite", overwrite = TRUE)
# edb <- EnsDb("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Workflows/EnsDb_Hsapiens_v97.sqlite")

library(ensembldb)
edb <- EnsDb("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Workflows/EnsDb_Hsapiens_v97.sqlite")

gene.symb <- sub("__chr.*$", "", rownames(sce.muraro))
gene.ids <- mapIds(edb, keys=gene.symb, keytype="SYMBOL", column="GENEID")

# Removing duplicated genes or genes without Ensembl IDs.
keep <- !is.na(gene.ids) & !duplicated(gene.ids)
sce.muraro <- sce.muraro[keep,]
rownames(sce.muraro) <- gene.ids[keep]

## Quality control----------------------------------------------------------------------
unfiltered <- sce.muraro

# The dataset lacks mitochondrial genes so related qc is not required
# For batch D28, there is a high-proportion of low-quality cells
# They can be removed using a shared median and MAD from the other batches
library(scater)
stats <- perCellQCMetrics(sce.muraro)
qc <- quickPerCellQC(stats, percent_subsets="altexps_ERCC_percent",
    batch=sce.muraro$donor, subset=sce.muraro$donor!="D28")
sce.muraro <- sce.muraro[,!qc$discard]

colData(unfiltered) <- cbind(colData(unfiltered), stats)
unfiltered$discard <- qc$discard

# Distribution of each QC metric across cells from each donor in the Muraro pancreas dataset. Each point represents a cell and is colored according to whether that cell was discarded.
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="donor", y="sum", colour_by="discard") +
        scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Total count"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="donor", y="detected", colour_by="discard") +
        scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Detected features"),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="donor", y="altexps_ERCC_percent",
        colour_by="discard") + ggtitle("ERCC percent"),
    ncol=2
)

# Causes of removal
colSums(as.matrix(qc))

## Normalization---------------------------------------------------------------------
library(scran)
set.seed(1000)
clusters <- quickCluster(sce.muraro)
sce.muraro <- computeSumFactors(sce.muraro, clusters=clusters)
sce.muraro <- logNormCounts(sce.muraro)

summary(sizeFactors(sce.muraro))

# Relationship between the library size factors and the deconvolution size factors in the Muraro pancreas dataset.
plot(librarySizeFactors(sce.muraro), sizeFactors(sce.muraro), pch=16,
    xlab="Library size factors", ylab="Deconvolution factors", log="xy")

## Variance modelling-------------------------------------------------------------------
block <- paste0(sce.muraro$plate, "_", sce.muraro$donor)
dec.muraro <- modelGeneVarWithSpikes(sce.muraro, "ERCC", block=block)
top.muraro <- getTopHVGs(dec.muraro, prop=0.1)

# Per-gene variance as a function of the mean for the log-expression values in the Muraro pancreas dataset. Each point represents a gene (black) with the mean-variance trend (blue) fitted to the spike-in transcripts (red) separately for each donor.
par(mfrow=c(8,4))
blocked.stats <- dec.muraro$per.block
for (i in colnames(blocked.stats)) {
    current <- blocked.stats[[i]]
    plot(current$mean, current$total, main=i, pch=16, cex=0.5,
        xlab="Mean of log-expression", ylab="Variance of log-expression")
    curfit <- metadata(current)
    points(curfit$mean, curfit$var, col="red", pch=16)
    curve(curfit$trend(x), col='dodgerblue', add=TRUE, lwd=2)
}

## Data integration--------------------------------------------------------------------
library(batchelor)
set.seed(1001010)
merged.muraro <- fastMNN(sce.muraro, subset.row=top.muraro, 
    batch=sce.muraro$donor)

# Using the proportion of variance lost as a diagnostic measure
metadata(merged.muraro)$merge.info$lost.var

## Dimensionality reduction------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(100111)
merged.muraro <- runTSNE(merged.muraro, dimred="corrected")

## Clustering----------------------------------------------------------------------
snn.gr <- buildSNNGraph(merged.muraro, use.dimred="corrected")
colLabels(merged.muraro) <- factor(igraph::cluster_walktrap(snn.gr)$membership)

tab <- table(Cluster=colLabels(merged.muraro), CellType=sce.muraro$label)

library(pheatmap)
# Heatmap of the frequency of cells from each cell type label in each cluster.

table(Cluster=colLabels(merged.muraro), Donor=merged.muraro$batch)

# Each point represents a cell that is colored by cluster (left) or batch (right).
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotTSNE(merged.muraro, colour_by="label"),
    plotTSNE(merged.muraro, colour_by="batch"),
    ncol=2
)

# Save the processed sce.muraro object
saveRDS(sce.muraro, "OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.muraro_processed.rds")
```

## Segerstolpe human pancreas (Smart-seq2)

```{r}
## Data loading--------------------------------------------------------------------
library(scRNAseq)
# sce.seger <- SegerstolpePancreasData()
# saveRDS(sce.seger, "OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.seger.rds")
sce.seger <- readRDS("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.seger.rds")

# library(AnnotationHub)
# edb <- AnnotationHub()[["AH73881"]]
library(ensembldb)
edb <- EnsDb("OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Workflows/EnsDb_Hsapiens_v97.sqlite")

symbols <- rowData(sce.seger)$symbol
ens.id <- mapIds(edb, keys=symbols, keytype="SYMBOL", column="GENEID")
ens.id <- ifelse(is.na(ens.id), symbols, ens.id)

# Removing duplicated rows.
keep <- !duplicated(ens.id)
sce.seger <- sce.seger[keep,]
rownames(sce.seger) <- ens.id[keep]

# Simplifying the names of some of the relevant column metadata fields
emtab.meta <- colData(sce.seger)[,c("cell type", "disease",
    "individual", "single cell well quality")]
colnames(emtab.meta) <- c("CellType", "Disease", "Donor", "Quality")
colData(sce.seger) <- emtab.meta

sce.seger$CellType <- gsub(" cell", "", sce.seger$CellType)
sce.seger$CellType <- paste0(
    toupper(substr(sce.seger$CellType, 1, 1)),
    substring(sce.seger$CellType, 2))

## Quality control--------------------------------------------------------------------
unfiltered <- sce.seger

# Removing low quality cells marked by the authors
# Also performing additional quality control to remove cells with very low counts and number of detected features
# For batches that have a majority of low-quality cells, we use the other batches to define an appropritate threshold via subset
low.qual <- sce.seger$Quality == "OK, filtered"

library(scater)
stats <- perCellQCMetrics(sce.seger)
qc <- quickPerCellQC(stats, percent_subsets="altexps_ERCC_percent",
    batch=sce.seger$Donor,
    subset=!sce.seger$Donor %in% c("H6", "H5"))

sce.seger <- sce.seger[,!(qc$discard | low.qual)]

colData(unfiltered) <- cbind(colData(unfiltered), stats)
unfiltered$discard <- qc$discard

# Distribution of each QC metric across cells from each donor of the Segerstolpe pancreas dataset. Each point represents a cell and is colored according to whether that cell was discarded.
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="Donor", y="sum", colour_by="discard") +
        scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Total count") +
        theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="Donor", y="detected", colour_by="discard") +
        scale_y_log10() + ggtitle("Detected features") +
        theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)),
    plotColData(unfiltered, x="Donor", y="altexps_ERCC_percent",
        colour_by="discard") + ggtitle("ERCC percent") +
        theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)),
    ncol=2
)

colSums(as.matrix(qc))

## Normalization-------------------------------------------------------------------
# We don’t normalize the spike-ins at this point as there are some cells with no spike-in counts.
library(scran)
clusters <- quickCluster(sce.seger)
sce.seger <- computeSumFactors(sce.seger, clusters=clusters)
sce.seger <- logNormCounts(sce.seger)

summary(sizeFactors(sce.seger))

# Relationship between the library size factors and the deconvolution size factors in the Segerstolpe pancreas dataset.
plot(librarySizeFactors(sce.seger), sizeFactors(sce.seger), pch=16,
    xlab="Library size factors", ylab="Deconvolution factors", log="xy")

## Variance modelling----------------------------------------------------------------
for.hvg <- sce.seger[,librarySizeFactors(altExp(sce.seger)) > 0 & sce.seger$Donor!="H1"]
dec.seger <- modelGeneVarWithSpikes(for.hvg, "ERCC", block=for.hvg$Donor)
chosen.hvgs <- getTopHVGs(dec.seger, n=2000)

# Per-gene variance as a function of the mean for the log-expression values in the Grun pancreas dataset. Each point represents a gene (black) with the mean-variance trend (blue) fitted to the spike-in transcripts (red) separately for each donor.
par(mfrow=c(3,3))
blocked.stats <- dec.seger$per.block
for (i in colnames(blocked.stats)) {
    current <- blocked.stats[[i]]
    plot(current$mean, current$total, main=i, pch=16, cex=0.5,
        xlab="Mean of log-expression", ylab="Variance of log-expression")
    curfit <- metadata(current)
    points(curfit$mean, curfit$var, col="red", pch=16)
    curve(curfit$trend(x), col='dodgerblue', add=TRUE, lwd=2)
}

## Dimensionality reduction----------------------------------------------------------------
# We pick the first 25 PCs for downstream analysis
library(BiocSingular)
set.seed(101011001)
sce.seger <- runPCA(sce.seger, subset_row=chosen.hvgs, ncomponents=25)
sce.seger <- runTSNE(sce.seger, dimred="PCA")

## Clustering---------------------------------------------------------------------
library(bluster)
clust.out <- clusterRows(reducedDim(sce.seger, "PCA"), NNGraphParam(), full=TRUE)
snn.gr <- clust.out$objects$graph
colLabels(sce.seger) <- clust.out$clusters

# There is a strong donor effect. 
# It might be due to differences in cell type composition between donors.
# More appropriately, it can be technical difference in plate processing or uninteresting genotypic differences (which can be removed using fastMNN)
tab <- table(Cluster=colLabels(sce.seger), Donor=sce.seger$Donor)
library(pheatmap)
# Heatmap of the frequency of cells from each donor in each cluster.
pheatmap(log10(tab+10), color=viridis::viridis(100))

# Each point represents a cell that is colored by cluster (left) or batch (right).
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotTSNE(sce.seger, colour_by="label"),
    plotTSNE(sce.seger, colour_by="Donor"),
    ncol=2
)

## Data integration------------------------------------------------------------------
# Repeating the clustering after running fastMNN() on the donors.
# It yields a more coherent set of clusters where each cluster contains contributions from all donors.
library(batchelor)

set.seed(10001010)
corrected <- fastMNN(sce.seger, batch=sce.seger$Donor, subset.row=chosen.hvgs)

set.seed(10000001)
corrected <- runTSNE(corrected, dimred="corrected")

colLabels(corrected) <- clusterRows(reducedDim(corrected, "corrected"), NNGraphParam())

tab <- table(Cluster=colLabels(corrected), Donor=corrected$batch)
tab

# t-SNE after batch correction across donors. Each point represents a cell and is colored by the assigned cluster identity.
gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plotTSNE(corrected, colour_by="label"),
    plotTSNE(corrected, colour_by="batch"),
    ncol=2
)

## Multi-sample comparisons-------------------------------------------------------------
# As the dataset contains both healthy donors and those with type II diabetes, it can be interesting to identify genes that are differentially expressed upon disease in each cell type
# We'll use the author-provided annotation rather than determining the cell type for each of our clusters
summed <- aggregateAcrossCells(sce.seger, 
    ids=colData(sce.seger)[,c("Donor", "CellType")])
summed

# Using the voom pipeline from the limma package
# It uses sample weights to better account for the variations in the precision of each pseudo-bulk profile
summed.beta <- summed[,summed$CellType=="Beta"]

library(edgeR)
y.beta <- DGEList(counts(summed.beta), samples=colData(summed.beta),
    genes=rowData(summed.beta)[,"symbol",drop=FALSE])
y.beta <- y.beta[filterByExpr(y.beta, group=y.beta$samples$Disease),]
y.beta <- calcNormFactors(y.beta)

design <- model.matrix(~Disease, y.beta$samples)
v.beta <- voomWithQualityWeights(y.beta, design)
fit.beta <- lmFit(v.beta)
fit.beta <- eBayes(fit.beta, robust=TRUE)

res.beta <- topTable(fit.beta, sort.by="p", n=Inf,
    coef="Diseasetype II diabetes mellitus")
# Insulin is downregulated in beta cells in the disease state
head(res.beta)

# MA plot
# MA plots for the beta cell pseudo-bulk profiles. Each MA plot is generated by comparing the corresponding pseudo-bulk profile against the average of all other profiles
par(mfrow=c(5, 2))
for (i in colnames(y.beta)) {
    plotMD(y.beta, column=i)
}
# Easier to just re-run it with plot=TRUE than to try to make the plot from 'v.beta'.
# Diagnostic plots for voom after estimating observation and quality weights from the beta cell pseudo-bulk profiles. The left plot shows the mean-variance trend used to estimate the observation weights, while the right plot shows the per-sample quality weights.
voomWithQualityWeights(y.beta, design, plot=TRUE)

# Save the processed dataset
saveRDS(sce.seger, "OSCA_datasets/OSCA_Basics/sce.seger_processed.rds")
```
